source.title: Safety and accuracy follow different scaling laws in clinical large language models
source.authors: Sebastian Wind; Tri-Thien Nguyen; Jeta Sopa; Mahshad Lotfinia; S. Bickelhaupt; M. Uder; H. Köstler; Gerhard Wellein; S. Nebelung; D. Truhn; Andreas K. Maier; S. T. Arasteh

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream radiology question-answering accuracy across model sizes and deployment conditions, rather than testing held-out pretraining loss or fitting the original scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports model-size and family comparisons for accuracy, but it does not report cross-entropy loss, power-law fits, small-run extrapolations, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its retrieval, evidence, self-consistency, and ensemble results do not directly test the claim versions unless they bear on downstream accuracy across scale.
record.test_reason: The study plots closed-book accuracy on a 200-question radiology multiple-choice benchmark against log parameter count for 34 models (0.5B–685B) in seven families (Fig. 4a). That is a downstream-performance-versus-scale result in a new clinical setting, so it bears on V6. It reports no loss, no fits and no extrapolation, and compares heterogeneous released models, not controlled runs. It therefore says nothing on V1–V5 or V7. T3 fits better than T2: this is a new setting and benchmark, not a different method aimed at the original question.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that parameter count and family affect closed-book performance, and that larger or stronger families start from better baselines, so scale is not irrelevant. Deployment condition, however, explains more variance than family, and scale does not substitute for clean clinical evidence for either accuracy or safety.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares downstream clinical question-answering accuracy across model sizes and deployment settings; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit the original power-law relationships.
record.method_sensitivity: Deployment condition strongly changes accuracy: clean clinician-written evidence raises panel accuracy, while family differences narrow under clean evidence.

fits_no_version.finding: The safety metrics (high-risk error rate, dangerous overconfidence) are plotted against parameter count (Fig. 4b,c). The paper says model-side scaling does not remove dangerous overconfidence. In a two-way decomposition, deployment condition explains 43/45/38% of variance in accuracy, high-risk error and dangerous overconfidence, versus 9/8/17% for model family.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Clinical safety-error rates do not scale with model size the way accuracy does; deployment condition dominates.

record.problems: For the scaling question, the study reports downstream accuracy rather than held-out loss, gives no power-law fit or extrapolation test, and does not provide uncertainty for the reported family-level accuracy values. The benchmark is one 200-question, text-based multiple-choice radiology dataset.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results directly testing the claim versions were left out. Retrieval, self-consistency, and ensemble metrics not tied to size-based downstream prediction were not cataloged as rows for this claim.

Whether the improvement follows a predictable or fitted law. Any link to pretraining loss. Other downstream tasks beyond one 200-question radiology benchmark. Controlled scaling at fixed data and recipe: the models are heterogeneous releases.

missing.what: Within-family size series for Qwen3 4B/14B/32B accuracy: closed-book 68.9/78.9/79.9, conflict evidence 92.9/94.4/93.9, standard RAG 74.3/81.5/84.0.
Per-model accuracy against log parameter count for closed-book and clean evidence, with within-family curves (collapse to a ceiling under clean evidence). Supp. Table 7 gives the parameter counts.

record.verdict_notes: The title's 'scaling laws' is used loosely: no power-law fit is made. Most of the reader's rows were condition or family comparisons and are relinked to none. The reader's supports label citing R4 and R5 relied on family aggregates, which do not isolate scale. Its limits_scope label rested on condition effects; it is restated here using the size-specific numbers from the text.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss and its scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and training tokens, and scaling of either quantity with compute.
Comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling-law form in other modalities or training regimes.

The study tests accuracy on one clinical radiology benchmark across model sizes and conditions, but not prediction from pretraining loss, broad downstream task coverage, or extrapolation to larger runs.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices, and deviations from a fitted single power law.

relationships.condition: Closed-book prompting, accuracy against parameter count across the panel and within the Qwen3 family
relationships.reason: R3: accuracy rises from 41.5 at the smallest to 88.4 at the largest scale. Per the text, Qwen3 4B, 14B and 32B score 68.9, 78.9 and 79.9 (Supp. Table 3; not a row). No fitted law is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased from 41.5 at the smallest scale to 88.4 at the largest, while Qwen3 scores increased from 68.9 to 78.9 to 79.9.

relationships.condition: When clean or conflict evidence is supplied in the prompt
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not rows. Families collapse to a 90.4–97.0 ceiling band under clean evidence (Fig. 4a). Qwen3 under conflict evidence is non-monotonic in size: 92.9 (4B), 94.4 (14B), 93.9 (32B). The scale gain largely vanishes depending on the deployment condition.
relationships.display_finding: Clean evidence brought model families into a 90.4–97.0 ceiling band, while conflicting evidence gave Qwen3 scores of 92.9, 94.4 and 93.9 at 4B, 14B and 32B.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Closed-book comparisons across the model-size panel
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports accuracy ranging from 41.5 at the smallest scale to 88.4 at the largest and says parameter count influenced closed-book performance; this is evidence of a scale-associated performance pattern, but not of a fitted predictive law (R3–R5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Across deployment conditions, especially clean-evidence prompting
reader_labels.reason: Clean evidence substantially raises accuracy for the panel and yields high family-level accuracy across families, while the paper says deployment condition explains more variance than family; scale alone is therefore not a sufficient predictor of the measured downstream outcome (R1–R2, R6–R12).
